The mockup was showing a real home directory

`docs/design/timeline.html` pinned the detail pane's layout with the path it
happened to be looking at the day it was written, and that path had a username
in it. Eight lines further down the same file already writes `/Users/…`, and
every other path in the repository is `/Users/x`, `/Users/me` or
`/Users/someone` — the mockup was the one place a real one survived.

The screenshots beside it are checked optically before they are installed;
nothing was checking the source. This is the only occurrence in the tree,
binaries included. `Cargo.toml`'s `authors` field stays: an author's name and
address are published with the crate on purpose, and are not a leak.

The screenshots, retakeable by a script instead of an afternoon

The four images in the readme go stale on every release — the app bar prints
its version into all of them — and the last set went out reading v1.1.0
because it had been shot from a development build. Retaking them is an hour of
driving a WebView through the accessibility API and blurring a home directory
out of the result, and the hour is spent rediscovering the same four things.

So the working version of that hour is in the repository. `bin/update.sh`
launches the app, pauses capture, switches to light, shoots the timeline, the
risk review and the timeline under each of the two filters, restores the theme
and capture, blurs every home directory, reads each image back to prove none
survived, and installs them. Nothing is installed unless every image passes the
read-back.

The four things, each written down beside what to do instead:

Vision's bounding box for a *substring* is not usable at 13px. It is honest
about it

A readme about the program, not about how it got here

The top of the file had become a changelog. Thirty lines of blockquote said
what v1.2 answered, then what v1.1 had changed, then which phase declined the
update check and which one cut the Linux build — before the first sentence
saying what the program is. The limitations read the same way: every entry
carried the phase that discovered it. All of it is true and none of it is what
someone arriving at the repository is trying to find out, and every word of it
is already in docs/README.md, which is where a history belongs.

So the history goes and the claims stay. The loopback guarantee keeps its two
tests, the two lanes keep the diagram and the tool_use_id join, and each
limitation keeps the ADR it rests on — it just no longer says when it was
decided. The one piece of the blockquote that was the program rather than its
history is the local model, and it is now a subsection of How it works.

Point the cask at v1.2.0

The checksum is the released artifact's, read from that release's SHA256SUMS —
a local build is not byte-identical, and publishing its checksum would hand
everybody a cask that refuses to install.

Put both verdicts where a reader is looking, and name the columns

Phase 13 shipped a second opinion that vanished at the moment it was most
wanted. Clicking a scored command in the risk view opened the detail pane, and
the verdict that sent the reader there was not in it. `@model-risk:>=4` returned
a list of commands with no visible reason for being in it. Reading that back
raised the question the phase had not asked: the *rules* were no more visible
than the model. `@risk:high` narrowed the timeline to ten rows and left the
reader to work out which rule had put each of them there.

Both verdicts are now columns in the timeline and blocks in the detail pane,
and they are never the same column. A rule's severity is a word in the risk
page's red and amber; a model's score is a digit in the second opinion's own
hue. ADR-0013 says a reader must be able to tell at a glance which produced a
number, and one shared column would be the fastest way to lose that. They also
rarely both appear: th

Phase 13: ADR-0013, the documentation, and the numbers so far

ADR-0013 records the four decisions the phase rested on and, more usefully, the
two rejections that would have been most tempting: letting the model raise a
severity — which would put a prompt injection's output into the numbers a
reviewer trusts — and downloading the model behind a switch, which would mean
deleting the egress check ADR-0008 is enforced by.

PRIVACY.md gains the paragraph task 13.11 asks for: the model is local, the
prompt is never transmitted, and it reads `input_summary` — the redacted
projection every other view reads — so the analysis adds **no new place a
secret can go**. database.md documents `llm_verdict` as the fourth table
recomputation cannot recover, beside the dismissal, the deletion and the
sighting. The README states the trade in its own words: 3.1 GB against a 166 MB
store, and a model that is wrong sometimes.

The phase file is filled in, including the parts that are not flattering.

Phase 13: a call arrives twice, and was being analysed twice

ADR-0009's central fact, costing something new. The transcript lane creates the
row and the OTLP lane completes it, so the live sink fires twice for one call,
both times with the same command — and the live path analysed it both times.
The primary key made the second write a REPLACE, so nothing was ever wrong;
what it cost was 1.25 seconds of inference to overwrite an answer with itself,
on every call witnessed by both lanes.

`observe` now claims the id first. In memory rather than a lookup in
`llm_verdict`, because this runs on the ingestion thread and that thread has no
read connection — giving it one to answer a question the backfill already
answers correctly would be the wrong trade. The store stays the authority, and
`pending` remains what stops the backfill redoing anything.

The set is cleared rather than evicted when it fills. An LRU would be right if
forgetting produced wrong data; it produces at most one repea

Phase 13: the bundle assertions, and the unsigned path that never worked

`just verify-bundle` now reads the shipped binary rather than trusting the
build's configuration, and both new checks pass on the real universal artifact:

    == linked libraries (ADR-0008, task 13.4) ==
        ok: no libcurl, no TLS library
    == deployment target (task 13.18) ==
        arm64  minos 11.0 (config says 11.0)
        x86_64 minos 11.0 (config says 11.0)

Getting there found a pre-existing bug the justfile's own comment denied. It
says an unset `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` produces an unsigned bundle that "still
builds". It did not: `just` cannot conditionally export, so the variable
reaches the bundler *present and empty*, and Tauri 2.11 reads that as "sign
with the identity ``" and fails with `: no identity found`. A machine without
the certificate got no bundle at all. `bundle` now unsets it when empty, and
the comment says why the indirection is load-bearing.

The universal build, which task 13.

Phase 13: the two filters, and the guarantee re-checked with llama.cpp in it

The egress test's own comment says the guarantee is only as good as what runs
inside it, so the workload now runs Phase 13's reads too: the prompt rendered,
the GGUF header read on a file that is not a model, verdicts written and read
back, and the timeline narrowed by them. It still opens no non-loopback socket
with llama.cpp linked into the test binary — which is the exit criterion, and
the half that matters, because a library that opened a socket on load would be
seen by the census whether or not this test called it.

One check the manifest scan structurally cannot make: libcurl reaches the
binary through CMake, not through Cargo. Saying otherwise in `OUTBOUND_CLIENTS`
would be theatre, so it is named in a constant that says where it *is* checked,
and a test asserts `just verify-bundle` still contains that check — because the
thing guarding the release is a `grep` inside a shell recipe, and deleting th

Phase 13 (part 3): the window, and the section that is not the rules

Status → Model points at a `.gguf`, shows what the file turned out to be, and
prints the `curl` line toolog will never run. It is honest about three
different kinds of nothing that look alike from a distance and lead to
completely different next steps: no model configured, a path that is not a
model, and a build with no inference compiled in.

The risk view gains one section, and its whole design is separation. Everything
above it is deterministic — a rule with an id, conditions anyone can read, a
severity that means the same thing every time. This is a 4.6B model's opinion.
So it sits on its own surface with its own border, it draws scores as digits on
the histogram's magnitude ramp rather than in the rules' red and amber, it uses
none of the four severity words, and it states the model and prompt that
produced it in words. A test asserts all of that, because "a reader must be
able to tell at a glance which numb

Phase 13 (part 2): the examination, and the floor that moved to 11.0

The resident half. A model configured in `prefs.json` loads on its own thread —
hashing 3.1 GB is 1.5 seconds and a menu-bar app must not take that long to
appear — and two threads then work: a backfill oldest-first through the calls
no rule matched, and a queue for calls as they arrive.

The backfill's queue is the store, not a `VecDeque`. Each batch asks which
calls this (model, prompt) pair has no verdict for, which makes it survive a
restart, unable to drift from what was recorded, and coordinated with the live
path for free. The live path never blocks ingestion: a full queue drops the
call, because the backfill will reach it anyway.

**The macOS floor moves 10.15 → 11.0**, and it is now written in four places
that have to agree. `.cargo/config.toml` and CI set both MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET
and CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET — the first reaches rustc, the second reaches
ggml, and without it ggml compiles bel

Phase 13 (part 1): a model, a prompt, and somewhere to put a verdict

The storage and inference core, with the two risks the phase named measured
before anything was built on them.

**The universal build holds.** Task 13.19 called it the risk that could sink
the phase, and it does not: a cold llama.cpp build is 29.8s for aarch64 and
23.5s for x86_64 on an M4 Pro, both link no libcurl, and `lipo` produces a
universal binary. `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` and `CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`
both go in a workspace `.cargo/config.toml`; `otool -l` confirms minos 11.0.
An `inference` feature exists as the reserved fallback and is on by default,
because a feature CI never builds is a feature that rots.

**The engine works on the real store**: 50 unmatched Bash commands, 0 schema
failures, 476 ms to load, 1,249 ms per call — a 3,618-call backfill in 75
minutes. Two things the spike found and the code now depends on:

`llama_sampler_sample` accepts the token into the chain itself. Calling
`accept

Fix the cask Homebrew refuses to load, and the check that missed it

`brew tap zaghaghi/tap` failed on the v1.1.0 cask: `depends_on macos:
:catalina` is disabled — Homebrew's version table no longer reaches back to
10.15, and brew itself now requires macOS 14. `verified:` on the `url`
stanza is deprecated in the same release.

`just cask-check` said "no offenses" about both, because it ran `brew style`,
which is RuboCop and does not load the cask. It now runs `brew readall`
first, which loads it for every platform — the same thing `brew tap` and a
user's install do. Verified by putting the broken stanza back: the old check
passed it, the new one fails it.

The cask now says `depends_on :macos` with no version. The bundle's own
LSMinimumSystemVersion is 10.15 and macOS will not launch below it, which is
the real floor and enforces itself; naming a version Homebrew still knows
would claim a *higher* floor than the app has and refuse to install on
machines where it runs.

The rules only find what someone thought to write a rule for. Measured on

Four decisions the phase rests on:

toolog gains no network capability. ADR-0008 is the tool's central claim and
the egress test forbids an HTTP client structurally, so the user brings the
GGUF and toolog is pointed at a path. That extends to C: llama.cpp's
LLAMA_CURL has defaulted on in some versions and would be invisible to a
manifest check, so the phase asserts `otool -L` on the shipped binary lists

Release v1.1.0

Phases 9–12 and the fixes that followed them:

  9  the usage and live views removed; toolog captures cost and reports
     none of it (ADR-0010)
 10  seven filter dropdowns became one @key:value query bar, an activity
     histogram that sets the range as well as showing it, and a detail
     pane that closes three ways
 11  the risk review from 2,314 ms to 95 ms, a summary whose columns add
     up to it, and every rule visible with what it looks for (ADR-0011)
 12  a sighting ledger recording when a finding was first seen, and
     @risk / @rule in the timeline (ADR-0012)

Since: session grouping removed after use, a blue accent measured rather
than eyeballed, a System/Light/Dark switch, and a detail pane that
scrolls.

The bundle test no longer asserts the version against a literal. That
assertion read Cargo.toml and compared it to a hard-coded string, so it
failed on every release while checking nothing; it now checks the shape
the release workflow's tag comparis

Give the search row one height

The box, the time control and Export sat on one line at three different
heights: the box is `--text-base` in mono with `--s3` of vertical padding,
the other two are `--text-sm` with `--s2`, which computes to 32px against
26px. Centring three different heights reads as an accident rather than as
a row.

`align-items: stretch` rather than `center`, so the height comes from the box
— the control that sets it — and the other two follow. Their wrappers become
flex so the single child inside each fills them, rather than needing a
`height: 100%` with nothing to resolve against. The vertical padding on the
select and the button goes, since the row supplies it now; the horizontal
padding stays, because the text still needs room either side.

Add a theme switch: System, Light or Dark

Both themes were fully built and the only way to pick one was System Settings.
Status gains an Appearance control with three states, not two: macOS changes
appearance at sunset, and a switch would make the state most people want the
one they cannot pick.

The choice is remembered in the window's localStorage rather than in
`prefs.json`. `Prefs` is a file the resident process reads because it acts on
what is in it — notifications fire from the capture thread, redaction happens
on the write path — and nothing outside the window cares which theme it is
drawn in. Keeping it local also means it is applied synchronously at boot: a
round trip to Rust would paint a light frame and correct it a moment later,
every launch. The activity chart's collapsed state is remembered the same way.

The dark palette is now written twice — once behind `prefers-color-scheme` for
"follow the system", once behind `[data-theme="dark"]` for an explicit choice.
That

Four fixes: a pane that scrolls, no grouping, time beside the box, blue

**The detail pane did not scroll.** `.split` set `grid-template-columns` and
no rows, so the implicit row was `auto` — sized by whatever the pane held.
A long result body ran off the bottom of the window with no way down.
`grid-template-rows: minmax(0, 1fr)` tells the row it may be shorter than its
content, which is what `overflow-y: auto` inside it needs to mean anything.

**Session grouping is gone**, and so is its machinery: the collapse set, the
group and subagent headers, `Plan.grouped`, `timeline_groups`, `SessionGroup`,
`AgentGroup`, and the per-group queries that narrowed a filter to one session
and one agent. 738 lines out against 114 in. A `group=session` hash written by
v1.0 is read and dropped rather than rejected, so an old link still restores
the filter it carried. A subagent's calls are still identifiable — the row
says which agent made them — they are simply not nested.

**Time moved onto the

Give a rule an identity, and cut the prose off the risk page

**Rule identity.** A sighting keyed on `rule_id` alone let a rule keep its id,
change what it looks for, and inherit a `first_seen` describing the question
it used to ask — measured on a rule retuned from `rm -rf` to `dd if=`, which
matched nothing and still reported the original date. Migration 007 keys
sightings on `(rule_id, fingerprint)`, where the fingerprint hashes the rule's
scope and every field of its `[rule.match]`. A retuned rule starts again; a
renamed or re-graded one keeps its history, because neither is a different
question. Rows written before 007 are claimed for the current fingerprint on
the next review rather than reset — verified on the real store, all 193 dates
intact through the upgrade.

The fingerprint is written field by field, so the compiler cannot notice a new
condition being left out of it. A test can, and does.
